Name: fragmentation_knowledge_tax
Title: The Fragmentation Tax: Does Subword Tokenization Fragmentation Causally Impair Cross-Lingual Knowledge Access, Independent of Language Resource Level?
Short Hypothesis: Prior work shows tokenizers fragment non-Latin/morphologically-rich languages into many more tokens, framing this purely as a cost/efficiency/fairness problem. We hypothesize fragmentation is also a *knowledge-access* bottleneck: the more tokens an entity name is split into, the harder it is for the model to retrieve facts about that entity, because subject-entity information must be reassembled across many tokens before mid-layer 'concept binding'. Crucially, we predict this effect holds even after controlling for language and resource level (i.e., within-language, high vs. low fragmentation of the same entity), and is causally localized to early-layer subject-token aggregation.
Related Work: A large body of work (Petrov et al. 2023; Teklehaymanot & Nejdl 2025; Dixit & Dixit 2026 'Script Tax'; Shani et al. 2026) documents that tokenization inflates token counts 3-15x for non-Latin/morphologically-rich languages, framing this as computational/latency/cost/fairness inequity. Multilingual knowledge-probing work (X-FACTR, Jiang et al. 2020) measures cross-lingual factual retrieval and attributes gaps to resource level and decoding difficulty. Interpretability work (ROME/subject-token enrichment) shows early layers aggregate multi-token subject information at the last subject token. What is missing: a controlled *causal* link between fragmentation and knowledge retrieval accuracy that (a) disentangles fragmentation from language and resource-level confounds, and (b) localizes the mechanism to early-layer subject aggregation. We move from 'fragmentation costs money/time' to 'fragmentation loses knowledge', and provide a mechanistic and interventional account rather than a descriptive cost survey.
Abstract: Multilingual tokenizers are known to fragment non-Latin and morphologically-rich languages into many more subword tokens than English, a phenomenon widely characterized as a computational and fairness cost. We ask a different, mechanistic question: does fragmentation itself impair a model's ability to *retrieve factual knowledge* about an entity, independent of language or training-data resource level? We hypothesize a 'fragmentation tax' on knowledge access: because early transformer layers must reassemble a multi-token subject into a single concept representation before mid-layer factual lookup, entities split into more tokens are systematically harder to query. We test this with three complementary controls. First, a within-language design: we compare high- vs. low-fragmentation entities in the *same* language, controlling for entity popularity/frequency, so any effect cannot be explained by language resource level. Second, an orthographic-manipulation design: we render the same entity in fragmentation-lowering (transliteration, spacing) vs. fragmentation-raising variants and measure knowledge-retrieval accuracy shifts. Third, a causal-mechanism design using activation patching to test whether restoring a low-fragmentation subject's early-layer aggregated representation into a high-fragmentation run recovers the fact. Across four open multilingual models and a Wikidata-derived multilingual fact set, we quantify how retrieval accuracy scales with subject token count, isolate the causal early-layer locus, and test a training-free mitigation (subject-representation pooling / retokenization). This reframes tokenization inequity as a substantive knowledge-reliability problem and offers a concrete interpretability-grounded remedy.
Experiments: 1) Fact set construction: from Wikidata, select ~1000 subject-relation-object triples with entities that vary widely in token fragmentation. For each entity, record subject token count (fertility) under each model's tokenizer, entity popularity (Wikipedia pageviews / QID sitelink count) as a frequency proxy, and language(s). Build parallel cloze/QA prompts in ~8 languages (English, German, Spanish, Russian, Hindi, Arabic, Chinese, Japanese) with template + verification. 2) Descriptive scaling: on open models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Aya-23-8B, Gemma-2-9B), measure closed-book retrieval accuracy and confidence and regress on subject token count while including entity popularity, relation type, and language as covariates. Report the partial effect of fragmentation controlling for popularity/resource. 3) Within-language matched control: within each language, form matched pairs of entities equal in popularity bucket but differing in fragmentation; compare accuracy (paired test) — this removes resource-level confound. 4) Orthographic manipulation: for a subset, create fragmentation-lowering variants (Latin transliteration, inserted spaces, canonical spelling) and fragmentation-raising variants (diacritic/rare-char forms) of the SAME entity; measure accuracy delta as fragmentation changes, holding the underlying entity fixed. 5) Causal mechanism: using activation patching / interchange interventions, patch the last-subject-token early-layer residual state from a low-fragmentation run into a high-fragmentation run and test whether the correct object becomes recoverable; sweep layers to localize the aggregation locus (predict early layers). Compare to logit-lens tracking of when subject identity becomes decodable. 6) Mitigation: implement a training-free 'subject pooling' intervention (mean/attention-pool subject-token states into a single injected representation) or a retokenization/insert-space preprocessing; measure accuracy recovery and specificity (no degradation on low-fragmentation controls). Metrics: retrieval accuracy, fragmentation partial-regression coefficient, matched-pair accuracy gap, orthographic accuracy delta, patching recovery rate, mitigation net accuracy gain, and layer-localization curves.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Fragmentation and entity rarity are correlated; we address this via within-language matched pairs and orthographic manipulation of fixed entities, but residual confounding may remain and is reported. 2) Transliteration/spacing manipulations may alter entity identity or introduce artifacts; we validate that the model still recognizes the entity via a recognition check. 3) The effect may be small for highly popular entities; we stratify by popularity to detect where the tax is largest. 4) Activation-patching results can be model- and layer-specific; we report across four models and sweep layers. 5) Multi-token object prediction complicates accuracy scoring; we use first-token/answer-normalization and manual validation on a subset. 6) A null within-language result would still be informative, cleanly separating resource-level effects from tokenization effects.
